title: The Data Behind the Cafeteria Menu
passage:
The cafeteria at Mari's school wanted to reduce the amount of food thrown away after lunch. Staff began weighing leftovers from each dish and recording the results. After a month, one pattern looked obvious: vegetable dishes produced more waste than rice or bread. A quick response would have been to serve fewer vegetables. However, the nutrition teacher warned that the data showed what students left, not why they left it. The student council joined the investigation. They compared waste with menu type, serving size, weather, and the order in which dishes were placed on the serving line. They also conducted a short anonymous survey. The results complicated the original story. One vegetable dish was unpopular because it became watery when kept warm for too long. Another was generally liked, but the serving spoon was large, so students often took more than they wanted. On days when a new dish appeared, waste was high because students could not judge how much to take. The council tested several changes. For familiar vegetables, they used smaller serving spoons and allowed students to return for more. For new dishes, they offered a small tasting portion first. Kitchen staff also changed the preparation time of the watery dish so it spent less time warming. Waste fell during the test, but another issue appeared. Allowing second servings created a short line, and students with later lunch periods worried that popular dishes might run out. Staff therefore prepared a small reserve and monitored demand. Mari noticed that each improvement created a new condition to consider. The project was not a simple search for the single cause of waste. It was a system in which portion size, taste, timing, expectations, and food supply interacted. The school also had to avoid an unintended goal: reducing waste by making students take too little food. Nutrition mattered more than producing an impressive waste number. For that reason, the final report included two measures instead of one: leftover weight and the percentage of students who reported being satisfied with the meal. The council also tracked whether students returned for second servings. After a term, vegetable waste had decreased, while satisfaction remained roughly stable. The school considered this encouraging but did not call the project finished. Menus changed with the seasons, and new students would arrive the following year. Mari learned that numbers are powerful when they help people notice patterns, but a number does not explain itself. If the school had reacted only to the first chart, it might have reduced vegetables and claimed success while making lunches less healthy. Better decisions came from combining measurement with observation, questions, and small experiments. She also learned that a metric can influence behavior. Once people are told to minimize one number, they may find ways to improve it that do not serve the real purpose. The cafeteria's true goal was not the lightest trash bin. It was to provide nutritious meals that students would actually eat while wasting as little food as reasonably possible.

The project also changed how kitchen staff discussed unpopular food. Instead of saying that students simply disliked a dish, they began asking whether the problem involved taste, texture, temperature, portion size, or unfamiliarity. Those questions led to smaller and more focused experiments. One soup was served in smaller bowls because students often wanted only a taste. A vegetable side dish was placed earlier in the serving line so it was easier to notice before trays became full. Another recipe was left unchanged after surveys showed that a vocal minority disliked it but most students ate it. Mari learned that a complaint can be real without representing everyone. By separating different possible causes, the school avoided making one large change based on a single impression. None of the improvements was dramatic by itself, but together they reduced one source of misunderstanding. This mattered too.
translation:
真理の学校の食堂では、昼食後に捨てられる食品を減らすため、料理ごとの残り物を量って記録し始めました。一か月後、野菜料理の廃棄が米やパンより多いことが明らかになりました。単純に考えれば野菜を減らせばよいように見えますが、栄養担当の先生は『データが示すのは何を残したかで、なぜ残したかではない』と指摘しました。生徒会は、献立、盛り付け量、天気、配膳順などと廃棄量を比べ、匿名アンケートも行いました。すると、ある野菜料理は保温時間が長く水っぽくなること、別の料理は味は好評でも大きなスプーンで取りすぎること、新しい料理では適量が分からず残しやすいことが分かりました。そこで小さなスプーン、追加のおかわり、新料理の少量試食、調理時間の変更などを試しました。廃棄は減りましたが、今度はおかわり列ができ、後半の時間帯で料理が不足する不安が出たため、少量の予備を用意しました。真理は、一つ改善すると新しい条件が現れ、この問題が単一原因ではなく、量、味、時間、期待、供給が関係する仕組みだと気づきました。また『廃棄を減らす』だけを目標にすると、生徒に少なすぎる量を取らせれば数字だけは良くなる危険もあります。そこで最終報告では廃棄重量だけでなく、食事への満足度とおかわり状況も測りました。一学期後、野菜の廃棄は減り、満足度はほぼ維持されました。ただし季節や新入生によって状況は変わるため、終了とは考えませんでした。真理は、数字はパターンを見つける力を持つ一方、数字自身が理由を説明するわけではないと学びます。最初のグラフだけで判断していれば、野菜を減らして数字を改善しながら昼食を不健康にしていたかもしれません。測定、観察、質問、小さな実験を組み合わせることでより良い判断ができます。そして本当の目的は『ごみ箱を最も軽くすること』ではなく、栄養のある食事を生徒が実際に食べ、無理のない範囲で無駄を減らすことでした。

この活動によって、厨房でも『残り物が多い料理＝生徒が嫌いな料理』とすぐ決めつけなくなりました。味、食感、温度、量、見慣れなさなど、別々の原因を考えるようになったのです。あるスープは少量だけ試したい生徒が多いため小さな器にし、野菜のおかずはトレーがいっぱいになる前に目に入りやすい位置へ移しました。別の料理は、一部の強い不満はあっても多くの生徒が食べていることが調査で分かり、変更しませんでした。真理は、一つの不満が本物であっても全員を代表するとは限らないと学びました。原因を分けて考えることで、印象だけをもとに大きく変更することを避けられました。個々の工夫は小さくても、合わせることで誤解の原因を一つずつ減らすことができました。 この点も重要でした。
